opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the basic approach is to take questions that people tend to have strong intuitions about, things like "when will we get human-level AI?" or "will progress be sudden or gradual?", and try to break them into smaller pieces that you can actually check against evidence.

So a lot of what we do is fairly unglamorous. Instead of asking "will there be a discontinuity in AI progress?" directly, we might ask: how often have there been discontinuities in technological progress historically? Then we go look at a whole bunch of trends, like ship speeds, bridge lengths, chess ratings, and so on, and try to measure how often something jumped well ahead of what you'd have predicted from the previous trend. That gives you a base rate that's at least somewhat grounded, and then you can argue about whether AI is likely to be different.

Another big strand is just asking people. We've run surveys of machine learning researchers, the people publishing at the big conferences, about when they expect various capabilities, what they think the risks are, and so on. I don't think experts are oracles about this. In fact, one of the interesting findings is how inconsistent the answers can be depending on how you frame the question. But it's still useful to know what the field collectively believes, and to track how that shifts over time.

More broadly, I'm trying to be careful about which arguments actually hold up. There are a lot of arguments in this space that feel compelling, and part of the work is laying them out step by step and asking, does this premise really follow? What would we expect to see if it were true? Sometimes the answer is that an argument is weaker than people assume, and sometimes it's stronger. Either way, it seems valuable to have the pieces written down so people can disagree about specific things rather than just vibes.

r001.rationale: It describes breaking broad questions about AI’s future into smaller, evidence-checkable questions, then using findings such as historical rates of technological discontinuity to inform the broader AI question.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, a lot of the questions people care about with AI's future seem at first like they're just too big or too speculative to say anything rigorous about. "When will we have human-level AI?" "Will it be dangerous?" "What will the economy look like?" And the temptation is either to throw up your hands or to just go with whatever your gut says. What we try to do at AI Impacts is take those enormous questions and break them down into smaller pieces that you actually can investigate empirically, and then see how far that gets you.

So, for instance, if you want to know how fast AI progress might go, one thing you can do is look at how fast progress has gone in other technologies historically. We've spent a surprising amount of time cataloging things like discontinuities in technological trends, where some metric suddenly jumped by what would normally be decades of progress. How often does that happen? What does it look like when it does? That gives you some base rate for thinking about whether AI might do something similar, rather than just arguing from intuition.

Another big part of it is surveys. We've run several surveys of machine learning researchers asking about their expectations, and those are interesting partly because of what they tell you and partly because of how inconsistent people's answers are. You can ask essentially the same question two different ways and get wildly different median estimates. That's informative in itself, about how much anyone really knows here.

I'd also say we try to be fairly honest about uncertainty. A lot of what we produce isn't "here's the answer," it's "here's what the evidence actually supports, here are the arguments, and here's where they fall apart when you look closely." I think that's valuable because so much of the discourse is people being very confident in opposite directions, and it helps to have somewhere that's just trying to lay out what's actually known.

And then the last thing is that I think it matters to look at the arguments themselves and not just the empirics. There are these standard arguments for why advanced AI might be catastrophic, and I've spent a fair amount of time trying to write out the strongest version of each one and asking how much weight it really bears. Sometimes the answer is less than I'd assumed, sometimes more. But the exercise of trying to make it precise is where a lot of the insight comes from.

astra-6.text:
I tend to start with a question that seems important for how the future of AI might go, and then ask whether there’s some smaller piece of it that we can actually get evidence about. It’s easy for discussions of AI to stay at the level of competing intuitions. We try to find places where those intuitions imply something you could check.

For example, if you’re wondering whether AI progress might be very abrupt, you can look at other technological developments and ask how often progress has involved large discontinuities, and under what circumstances. That won’t settle what happens with AI, but it can help constrain the stories we tell. Or you can ask researchers about their expectations, while being clear that a survey of expectations isn’t a measurement of the future.

So the approach is fairly empirical, where possible, and fairly piecemeal. We’re usually trying to make an important uncertainty a little smaller, rather than produce one comprehensive forecast of everything that’s going to happen.

sol-6.1.text:
At AI Impacts, we try to take these very big questions about the future of AI and break them down into smaller questions where we can actually find some evidence. It’s hard to directly investigate something like, “When will AI be able to do everything humans can do?” But you can ask what different people expect, what their expectations are based on, and whether there are historical cases that might help us understand a particular argument.

I tend to be interested in finding the points where people’s views depend on an assumption that we could investigate. If someone expects AI progress to be very abrupt, for instance, we can ask what would make it abrupt and what evidence would bear on that. The aim is to make our uncertainty more explicit and, where possible, replace a little of it with something we’ve learned.
